arXiv:2007.00224v3 [cs.LG] 21 Oct 2020

Debiased Contrastive Learning

Ching-Yao Chuang    Joshua Robinson    Lin Yen-Chen Affiliation: Antonio Torralba, Stefanie Jegelka Affiliation: CSAIL, Massachusetts Institute of Technology Affiliation: Cambridge, MA 02139, USA Affiliation: {cychuang, joshrob, yenchenl, torralba, stefje}@mit.edu
Abstract

A prominent technique for self-supervised representation learning has been to contrast semantically similar and dissimilar pairs of samples. Without access to labels, dissimilar (negative) points are typically taken to be randomly sampled datapoints, implicitly accepting that these points may, in reality, actually have the same label. Perhaps unsurprisingly, we observe that sampling negative examples from truly different labels improves performance, in a synthetic setting where labels are available. Motivated by this observation, we develop a debiased contrastive objective that corrects for the sampling of same-label datapoints, even without knowledge of the true labels. Empirically, the proposed objective consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art for representation learning in vision, language, and reinforcement learning benchmarks. Theoretically, we establish generalization bounds for the downstream classification task.

1 Introduction

Learning good representations without supervision has been a long-standing goal of machine learning. One such approach is self-supervised learning, where auxiliary learning objectives leverage labels that can be observed without a human labeler. For instance, in computer vision, representations can be learned from colorization [45], predicting transformations [10, 32], or generative modeling [24, 14, 3]. Remarkable success has also been achieved in the language domain [30, 25, 8].

Recently, self-supervised representation learning algorithms that use a contrastive loss have outperformed even supervised learning [15, 28, 19, 18, 2]. The key idea of contrastive learning is to contrast semantically similar (positive) and dissimilar (negative) pairs of data points, encouraging the representations ff of similar pairs (x,x+)(x,x^{+}) to be close, and those of dissimilar pairs (x,x−)(x,x^{-}) to be more orthogonal [33, 2]:

𝔼x,x+,{xi−}i=1N​[−log⁡ef​(x)T​f​(x+)ef​(x)T​f​(x+)+∑i=1Nef​(x)T​f​(xi−)].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x,x^{+},\{x^{-}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}}\left[-\log\frac{e^{f(x)^{T}f(x^{+})}}{e^{f(x)^{T}f(x^{+})}+\sum_{i=1}^{N}e^{f(x)^{T}f(x_{i}^{-})}}\right]. (1)

In practice, the expectation is replaced by the empirical estimate. For each training data point xx, it is common to use one positive example, e.g., derived from perturbations, and NN negative examples xi−x^{-}_{i}. Since true labels or true semantic similarity are typically not available, negative counterparts xi−x^{-}_{i} are commonly drawn uniformly from the training data. But, this means it is possible that x−x^{-} is actually similar to xx, as illustrated in Figure 2. This phenomenon, which we refer to as sampling bias, can empirically lead to significant performance drop. Figure 2 compares the accuracy for learning with this bias, and for drawing xi−x^{-}_{i} from data with truly different labels than xx; we refer to this method as unbiased (further details in Section 5.1).

However, the ideal unbiased objective is unachievable in practice since it requires knowing the labels, i.e., supervised learning. This dilemma poses the question whether it is possible to reduce the gap between the ideal objective and standard contrastive learning, without supervision. In this work, we demonstrate that this is indeed possible, while still assuming only access to unlabeled training data and positive examples. In particular, we develop a correction for the sampling bias that yields a new, modified loss that we call debiased contrastive loss. The key idea underlying our approach is to indirectly approximate the distribution of negative examples. The new objective is easily compatible with any algorithm that optimizes the standard contrastive loss. Empirically, our approach improves over the state of the art in vision, language and reinforcement learning benchmarks.

Our theoretical analysis relates the debiased contrastive loss to supervised learning: optimizing the debiased contrastive loss corresponds to minimizing an upper bound on a supervised loss. This leads to a generalization bound for the supervised task, when training with the debiased contrastive loss.

In short, this work makes the following contributions:

  • •

    We develop a new, debiased contrastive objective that corrects for the sampling bias of negative examples, while only assuming access to positive examples and the unlabeled data;

  • •

    We evaluate our approach via experiments in vision, language, and reinforcement learning;

  • •

    We provide a theoretical analysis of the debiased contrastive representation with generalization guarantees for a resulting classifier.

2 Related Work

Contrastive Representation Learning.

The contrastive loss has recently become a prominent tool in unsupervised representation learning, leading to state-of-the-art results. The main difference between different approaches to contrastive learning lies in their strategy for obtaining positive pairs. Examples in computer vision include random cropping and flipping [33], or different views of the same scene [40]. Chen et al. [2] extensively study verious data augmentation methods. For language, Logeswaran and Lee [28] treat the context sentences as positive samples to efficiently learn sentence representations. Srinivas et al. [37] improve the sample efficiency of reinforcement learning with representations learned via the contrastive loss. Computational efficiency has been improved by maintaining a dictionary of negative examples [18, 4]. Concurrently, Wang and Isola [42] analyze the asymptotic contrastive loss and propose new metrics to measure the representation quality. All of these works sample negative examples from p⁡(x)p(x).

Arora et al. [1] theoretically analyze the effect of contrastive representation learning on a downstream, “average” classification task and provide a generalization bound for the standard objective. They too point out the sampling bias as a problem, but do not propose any models to address it.

Positive-unlabeled Learning.

Since we approximate the contrastive loss with only unlabeed data from p⁡(x)p(x) and positive examples, our work is also related to Positive-Unlabeled (PU) learning, i.e., learning from only positive (P) and unlabeled (U) data. Common applications of PU learning are retrieval or outlier detection [13, 12, 11]. Our approach is related to unbiased PU learning, where the unlabeled data is used as negative examples, but down-weighted appropriately [26, 12, 11]. While these works focus on zero-one losses, we here address the contrastive loss, where existing PU estimators are not directly applicable.

3 Setup and Sampling Bias in Contrastive Learning

Contrastive learning assumes access to semantically similar pairs of data points (x,x+)(x,x^{+}), where xx is drawn from a data distribution p⁡(x)p(x) over 𝒳\mathcal{X}. The goal is to learn an embedding f:𝒳→ℝdf\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d} that maps an observation xx to a point on a hypersphere with radius 1/t1/t, where tt is the temperature scaling hyperparameter. Without loss of generality, we set t=1t=1 for all theoretical results.

Similar to [1], we assume an underlying set of discrete latent classes 𝒞\mathcal{C} that represent semantic content, i.e., similar pairs (x,x+)(x,x^{+}) have the same latent class. Denoting the distribution over classes by ρ⁡(c)\rho(c), we obtain the joint distribution px,c​(x,c)=p⁡(x|c)​ρ​(c)p_{x,c}(x,c)=p(x|c)\rho(c). Let h:𝒳→𝒞h\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{C} be the function assigning the latent class labels. Then px+​(x′)=p⁡(x′|h⁡(x′)=h⁡(x))p_{x}^{+}(x^{\prime})=p(x^{\prime}|h(x^{\prime})=h(x)) is the probability of observing x′x^{\prime} as a positive example for xx and px−​(x′)=p⁡(x′|h⁡(x′)≠h⁡(x))p_{x}^{-}(x^{\prime})=p(x^{\prime}|h(x^{\prime})\neq h(x)) the probability of a negative example. We assume that the class probabilities ρ⁡(c)=τ+\rho(c)=\tau^{+} are uniform, and let τ−=1−τ+\tau^{-}=1-\tau^{+} be the probability of observing any different class.

Note that to remain unsupervised in practice, our method and other contrastive losses only sample from the data distribution and a “surrogate” positive distribution, mimicked by data augmentations or context sentences [2, 28].

3.1 Sampling Bias

Intuitively, the contrastive loss will provide most informative representations for downstream classification tasks if the positive and negative pairs correspond to the desired latent classes. Hence, the ideal loss to optimize would be

LUnbiasedN​(f)=𝔼x∼p,x+∼px+xi−∼px−​[−log⁡ef​(x)T​f​(x+)ef​(x)T​f​(x+)+QN​∑i=1Nef​(x)T​f​(xi−)],\displaystyle L_{\textnormal{Unbiased}}^{N}(f)=\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim p,x^{+}\sim p_{x}^{+}\\ x_{i}^{-}\sim p_{x}^{-}\end{subarray}}\left[-\log\frac{e^{f(x)^{T}f(x^{+})}}{e^{f(x)^{T}f(x^{+})}+\frac{Q}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}e^{f(x)^{T}f(x_{i}^{-})}}\right], (2)

which we will refer to as the unbiased loss. Here, we introduce a weighting parameter QQ for the analysis. When the number NN of negative examples is finite, we set Q=NQ=N, in agreement with the standard contrastive loss. In practice, however, px−​(xi−)=p⁡(xi−|h⁡(xi−)≠h⁡(x))p_{x}^{-}(x^{-}_{i})=p(x^{-}_{i}|h(x^{-}_{i})\neq h(x)) is not accessible. The standard approach is thus to sample negative examples xi−x^{-}_{i} from the (unlabeled) p⁡(x)p(x) instead. We refer to the resulting loss as the biased loss LBiasedNL_{\textnormal{Biased}}^{N}. When drawn from p⁡(x)p(x), the sample xi−x^{-}_{i} will come from the same class as xx with probability τ+\tau^{+}.

Lemma 1 shows that in the limit, the standard loss LBiasedNL_{\textnormal{Biased}}^{N} upper bounds the ideal, unbiased loss.

Lemma 1.

For any embedding ff and finite NN, we have

LBiasedN​(f)≥LUnbiasedN​(f)+𝔼x∼p​[0∧log⁡𝔼x+∼px+​exp⁡f​(x)⊤​f​(x+)𝔼x−∼px−​exp⁡f​(x)⊤​f​(x−)]−e3/2​π2​N.\displaystyle L_{\textnormal{Biased}}^{N}(f)\geq L_{\textnormal{Unbiased}}^{N}(f)+\mathbb{E}_{x\sim p}\left[0\wedge\log\frac{\mathbb{E}_{x^{+}\sim p_{x}^{+}}\exp f(x)^{\top}f(x^{+})}{\mathbb{E}_{x^{-}\sim p_{x}^{-}}\exp f(x)^{\top}f(x^{-})}\right]-e^{3/2}\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2N}}. (3)

where a∧ba\wedge b denotes the minimum of two real numbers aa and bb.

Recent works often use large NN, e.g., N=65536N=65536 in [18], making the last term negligible. While, in general, minimizing an upper bound on a target objective is a reasonable idea, two issues arise here: (1) the smaller the unbiased loss, the larger is the second term, widening the gap; and (2) the empirical results in Figure 2 and Section 5 show that minimizing the upper bound LBiasedNL_{\textnormal{Biased}}^{N} and minimizing the ideal loss LUnbiasedNL_{\textnormal{Unbiased}}^{N} can result in very different learned representations.

4 Debiased Contrastive Loss

Next, we derive a loss that is closer to the ideal LUnbiasedNL_{\textnormal{Unbiased}}^{N}, while only having access to positive samples and samples from pp. Figure 2 shows that the resulting embeddings are closer to those learned with LUnbiasedNL_{\textnormal{Unbiased}}^{N}. We begin by decomposing the data distribution as

p⁡(x′)=τ+​px+​(x′)+τ−​px−​(x′).\displaystyle p(x^{\prime})=\tau^{+}p_{x}^{+}(x^{\prime})+\tau^{-}p_{x}^{-}(x^{\prime}).

An immediate approach would be to replace px−p_{x}^{-} in LUnbiasedNL_{\textnormal{Unbiased}}^{N} with px−​(x′)=(p⁡(x′)−τ+​px+​(x′))/τ−p_{x}^{-}(x^{\prime})=(p(x^{\prime})-\tau^{+}p_{x}^{+}(x^{\prime}))/\tau^{-} and then use the empirical counterparts for pp and px+p_{x}^{+}. The resulting objective can be estimated with samples from only pp and px+p_{x}^{+}, but is computationally expensive for large NN:

1(τ−)N​∑k=0N(Nk)​(−τ+)k​𝔼x∼p,x+∼px+{xi−}i=1k∼px+{xi−}i=k+1N∼p​[−log⁡ef​(x)T​f​(x+)ef​(x)T​f​(x+)+∑i=1Nef​(x)T​f​(xi−)],\displaystyle\frac{1}{(\tau^{-})^{N}}\sum_{k=0}^{N}\binom{N}{k}(-\tau^{+})^{k}\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim p,x^{+}\sim p_{x}^{+}\\ \{x_{i}^{-}\}_{i=1}^{k}\sim p_{x}^{+}\\ \{x_{i}^{-}\}_{i=k+1}^{N}\sim p\end{subarray}}\left[-\log\frac{e^{f(x)^{T}f(x^{+})}}{e^{f(x)^{T}f(x^{+})}+\sum_{i=1}^{N}e^{f(x)^{T}f(x_{i}^{-})}}\right], (4)

where {xi−}i=kj=∅\{x_{i}^{-}\}_{i=k}^{j}=\emptyset if k>jk>j. It also demands at least NN positive samples. To obtain a more practical form, we consider the asymptotic form as the number NN of negative examples goes to infinity.

Lemma 2.

For fixed QQ and N→∞N\rightarrow\infty, it holds that

𝔼x∼p,x+∼px+{xi−}i=1N∼px−N​[−log⁡ef​(x)T​f​(x+)ef​(x)T​f​(x+)+QN​∑i=1Nef​(x)T​f​(xi−)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim p,x^{+}\sim p_{x}^{+}\\ \{x_{i}^{-}\}_{i=1}^{N}\sim{p_{x}^{-}}^{N}\end{subarray}}\left[-\log\frac{e^{f(x)^{T}f(x^{+})}}{e^{f(x)^{T}f(x^{+})}+\frac{Q}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}e^{f(x)^{T}f(x_{i}^{-})}}\right] (5)
⟶\displaystyle\longrightarrow\; 𝔼x∼px+∼px+​[−log⁡ef​(x)T​f​(x+)ef​(x)T​f​(x+)+Qτ−​(𝔼x−∼p​[ef​(x)T​f​(x−)]−τ+​𝔼v∼px+​[ef​(x)T​f​(v)])].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim p\\ x^{+}\sim p_{x}^{+}\end{subarray}}\left[-\log\frac{e^{f(x)^{T}f(x^{+})}}{e^{f(x)^{T}f(x^{+})}+\frac{Q}{\tau^{-}}\big(\mathbb{E}_{x^{-}\sim p}[e^{f(x)^{T}f(x^{-})}]-\tau^{+}\mathbb{E}_{v\sim p_{x}^{+}}[e^{f(x)^{T}f(v)}]\big)}\right]. (6)

The limiting objective (6), which we denote by L~DebiasedQ\widetilde{L}_{\text{Debiased}}^{Q}, still samples examples x−x^{-} from pp, but corrects for that with additional positive samples vv. This essentially reweights positive and negative terms in the denominator.

The empirical estimate of L~DebiasedQ\widetilde{L}_{\text{Debiased}}^{Q} is much easier to compute than the straightforward objective (5). With NN samples {ui}i=1N\{u_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} from pp and MM samples {vi}i=1M\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M} from px+p_{x}^{+}, we estimate the expectation of the second term in the denominator as

g(x,{ui}i=1N,{vi}i=1M)=max{1τ−(1N∑i=1Nef​(x)T​f​(ui)−τ+1M∑i=1Mef​(x)T​f​(vi)),e−1/t}.\displaystyle g(x,\{u_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M})=\max\Big\{\frac{1}{\tau^{-}}\Big(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}e^{f(x)^{T}f(u_{i})}-\tau^{+}\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}e^{f(x)^{T}f(v_{i})}\Big),\;\;e^{-1/t}\Big\}. (7)

We constrain the estimator gg to be greater than its theoretical minimum e−1/t≤𝔼x−∼px−ef​(x)T​f​(xi−)e^{-1/t}\leq\mathbb{E}_{x^{-}\sim p_{x}^{-}}e^{f(x)^{T}f(x_{i}^{-})} to prevent calculating the logarithm of a negative number. The resulting population loss with fixed NN and MM per data point is

LDebiasedN,M​(f)=𝔼x∼p;x+∼px+{ui}i=1N∼pN{vi}i=1N∼px+M​[−log⁡ef​(x)T​f​(x+)ef​(x)T​f​(x+)+N​g​(x,{ui}i=1N,{vi}i=1M)],\displaystyle L_{\begin{subarray}{c}\textnormal{Debiased}\end{subarray}}^{N,M}(f)=\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim p;\,x^{+}\sim p_{x}^{+}\\ \{u_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}\sim p^{N}\\ \{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}\sim{p_{x}^{+}}^{M}\end{subarray}}\left[-\log\frac{e^{f(x)^{T}f(x^{+})}}{e^{f(x)^{T}f(x^{+})}+Ng\Big(x,\{u_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M}\Big)}\right], (8)

where, for simplicity, we set QQ to the finite NN. The class prior τ+\tau^{+} can be estimated from data [21, 6] or treated as a hyperparameter. Theorem 3 bounds the error due to finite NN and MM as decreasing with rate 𝒪(N−1/2+M−1/2)\mathcal{O}(N^{-1/2}+M^{-1/2}).

Theorem 3.

For any embedding ff and finite NN and MM, we have

|L~DebiasedN​(f)−LDebiasedN,M​(f)|≤e3/2τ−​π2​N+e3/2​τ+τ−​π2​M.\displaystyle\left|\widetilde{L}_{\textnormal{Debiased}}^{N}(f)-L_{\begin{subarray}{c}\textnormal{Debiased}\end{subarray}}^{N,M}(f)\right|\leq\frac{e^{3/2}}{\tau^{-}}\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2N}}+\frac{e^{3/2}\tau^{+}}{\tau^{-}}\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2M}}. (9)

Empirically, the experiments in Section 5 also show that larger NN and MM consistently lead to better performance. In the implementations, we use a full empirical estimate for LDebiasedN,ML_{\begin{subarray}{c}\textnormal{Debiased}\end{subarray}}^{N,M} that averages the loss over TT points xx, for finite NN and MM.

5 Experiments

In this section, we evaluate our new objective LDebiasedNL_{\textnormal{Debiased}}^{N} empirically, and compare it to the standard loss LBiasedNL_{\textnormal{Biased}}^{N} and the ideal loss LUnbiasedNL_{\textnormal{Unbiased}}^{N}. In summary, we observe the following: (1) the new loss outperforms state of the art contrastive learning on vision, language and reinforcement learning benchmarks; (2) the learned embeddings are closer to those of the ideal, unbiased objective; (3) both larger NN and large MM improve the performance; even one more positive example than the standard M=1M=1 can help noticeably. Detailed experimental settings can be found in the appendix. The code is available at https://github.com/chingyaoc/DCL.

5.1 CIFAR10 and STL10

First, for CIFAR10 [27] and STL10 [7], we implement SimCLR [2] with ResNet-50 [17] as the encoder architecture and use the Adam optimizer [23] with learning rate 0.0010.001. Following [2], we set the temperature to t=0.5t=0.5 and the dimension of the latent vector to 128128. All the models are trained for 400400 epochs and evaluated by training a linear classifier after fixing the learned embedding. Detailed experimental settings can be found in Appendix B.

To understand the effect of the sampling bias, we additionally consider an estimate of the ideal LUnbiasedNL_{\textnormal{Unbiased}}^{N}, which is a supervised version of the standard loss, where negative examples xi−x^{-}_{i} are drawn from the true px−p_{x}^{-}, i.e., using known classes. Since STL10 is not fully labeled, we only use the unbiased objective on CIFAR10.

Debiased Objective with M=1M=1.

For a fair comparison, i.e., no possible advantage from additional samples, we first examine our debiased objective with positive sample size M=1M=1 by setting v1=x+v_{1}=x^{+}. Then, our approach uses exactly the same data batch as the biased baseline. The debiased objective can be easily implemented by a slight modification of the code as Figure 3 shows. The results with different τ+\tau^{+} are shown in Figure 4(a,b). Increasing τ+\tau^{+} in Objective (7) leads to more correction, and gradually improves the performance in both benchmarks for different NN. Remarkably, with only a slight modification to the loss, we improve the accuracy of SimCLR on STL10 by 4.26%4.26\%. The performance of the debiased objective also improves by increasing the negative sample size NN.

Debiased Objective with M≥1M\geq 1.

By Theorem 3, a larger positive sample size MM leads to a better estimate of the loss. To probe its effect, we increase MM for all xx (e.g., MM times data augmentation) while fixing N=256N=256 and τ+=0.1\tau^{+}=0.1. Since increasing MM requires additional computation, we compare our debiased objective with biased SimCLR trained for 50% more epochs (600 epochs). The results for M=1,2,4,8M=1,2,4,8 are shown in Figure 4(c), and indicate that the performance of the debiased objective can indeed be further improved by increasing the number of positive samples. Surprisingly, with only one additional positive sample, the top-1 accuracy on STL10 can be significantly improved. We can also see that the debiased objective (M>1M>1) even outperforms a biased baseline trained with 50% more epochs.

Figure 5 shows t-SNE visualizations of the representations learned by the biased and debiased objectives (N=256N=256) on CIFAR10. The debiased contrastive loss leads to better class separation than the contrastive loss, and the result is closer to that of the ideal, unbiased loss.

5.2 ImageNet-100

Following [40], we test our approach on ImageNet-100, a randomly chosen subset of 100 classes of Imagenet. Compared to CIFAR10, ImageNet-100 has more classes and hence smaller class probabilities τ+\tau^{+}. We use contrastive multiview coding (CMC) [40] as our contrastive learning baseline, and M=1M=1 for a fair comparison. The results in Table 1 show that, although τ+\tau^{+} is small, our debiased objective still improves over the biased baseline.

5.3 Sentence Embeddings

Next, we test the debiased objective for learning sentence embeddings. We use the BookCorpus dataset [25] and examine six classification tasks: movie review sentiment (MR) [35], product reviews (CR) [20], subjectivity classification (SUBJ) [34], opinion polarity (MPQA) [43], question type classification (TREC) [41], and paraphrase identification (MSRP) [9]. Our experimental settings follow those for quick-thought (QT) vectors in [28]. In contrast to vision tasks, positive pairs here are chosen as neighboring sentences, which can form a different positive distribution from data augmentation. The minibatch of QT is constructed with a contiguous set of sentences, hence we can use the preceding and succeeding sentences as positive samples (M=2M=2). We retrain each model 3 times and show the average in Table 2. The debiased objective improves over the baseline in 44 out of 66 downstream tasks, verifying that our objective also works for a different modality.

5.4 Reinforcement Learning

Lastly, we consider reinforcement learning. We follow the experimental settings of Contrastive Unsupervised Representations for Reinforcement Learning (CURL) [37] to perform image-based policy control on top of the learned contrastive representations. Similar to vision tasks, the positive pairs are two different augmentations of the same image. We again set M=1M=1 for a fair comparison. Methods are tested at 100k environment steps on the DeepMind control suite [39], which consists of several continuous control tasks. We retrain each model 3 times and show the mean and standard deviation in Table 3. Our method consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art baseline (CURL) in different control tasks, indicating that correcting the sampling bias also improves the performance and data efficiency of reinforcement learning. In several tasks, the debiased approach also has smaller variance. With more positive examples (M=2M=2), we obtain further improvements.

5.5 Discussion

Class Distribution: Our theoretical results assume that the class distribution ρ\rho is close to uniform. In reality, this is often not the case, e.g., in our experiments, CIFAR10 and Imagenet-100 are the only two datasets with perfectly balanced class distributions. Nevertheless, our debiased objective still improves over the baselines even when the classes are not well balanced, indicating that the objective is robust to violations of the class balance assumption.

Positive Distribution: Even if we approximate the true positive distribution with a surrogate positive distribution, our debiased objective still consistently improves over the baselines. It is an interesting avenue of future work to adopt our debiased objective to a semi-supervised learning setting [44] where true positive samples are accessible.

6 Theoretical Analysis: Generalization Implications for Classification Tasks

Next, we relate the debiased contrastive objective to a supervised loss, and show how our contrastive learning approach leads to a generalization bound for a downstream supervised learning task.

We consider a supervised classification task 𝒯\mathcal{T} with KK classes {c1,…,cK}⊆𝒞\{c_{1},\dots,c_{K}\}\subseteq\mathcal{C}. After contrastive representation learning, we fix the representations f⁡(x)f(x) and then train a linear classifier q⁡(x)=W​f​(x)q(x)=Wf(x) on task 𝒯\mathcal{T} with the standard multiclass softmax cross entropy loss LSoftmax​(𝒯,q)L_{\textnormal{Softmax}}(\mathcal{T},q). Hence, we define the supervised loss for the representation ff as

LSup​(𝒯,f)=infW∈ℝK×dLSoftmax​(𝒯,W​f).\displaystyle L_{\textnormal{Sup}}(\mathcal{T},f)=\inf_{W\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times d}}L_{\textnormal{Softmax}}(\mathcal{T},Wf). (10)

In line with the approach of [1] we analyze the supervised loss of a mean classifier [36], where for each class cc, the rows of WW are set to the mean of the representations μc=𝔼x∼p(⋅|c)[f(x)]\mu_{c}=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim p(\cdot|c)}[f(x)]. We will use LSupμ​(𝒯,f)L_{\textnormal{Sup}}^{\mu}(\mathcal{T},f) as shorthand for its loss. Note that LSupμ​(𝒯,f)L_{\textnormal{Sup}}^{\mu}(\mathcal{T},f) is always an upper bound on LSup​(𝒯,f)L_{\textnormal{Sup}}(\mathcal{T},f). To allow for uncertainty about the task 𝒯\mathcal{T}, we will bound the average supervised loss for a uniform distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D} over KK-way classification tasks with classes in 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

LSup​(f)=𝔼𝒯∼𝒟​LSup​(𝒯,f).\displaystyle L_{\textnormal{Sup}}(f)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}\sim\mathcal{D}}L_{\textnormal{Sup}}(\mathcal{T},f). (11)

We begin by showing that the asymptotic unbiased contrastive loss is an upper bound on the supervised loss of the mean classifier.

Lemma 4.

For any embedding ff, whenever N≥K−1N\geq K-1 we have

LSup​(f)≤LSupμ​(f)≤L~DebiasedN​(f).L_{\textnormal{Sup}}(f)\leq L_{\textnormal{Sup}}^{\mu}(f)\leq\widetilde{L}_{\textnormal{Debiased}}^{N}(f).

Lemma 4 uses the asymptotic version of the debiased loss. Together with Theorem 3 and a concentration of measure result, it leads to a generalization bound for debiased contrastive learning, as we show next.

Generalization Bound.

In practice, we use an empirical estimate L^DebiasedN,M\widehat{L}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\textnormal{Debiased}\end{subarray}}^{N,M}, i.e., an average over TT data points xx, with MM positive and NN negative samples for each xx. Our algorithm learns an empirical risk minimizer f^∈arg​minf∈ℱ⁡L^DebiasedN,M​(f)\hat{f}\in\argmin_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\widehat{L}_{\textnormal{Debiased}}^{N,M}(f) from a function class ℱ\mathcal{F}. The generalization depends on the empirical Rademacher complexity ℛ𝒮​(ℱ)\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{F}) of ℱ\mathcal{F} with respect to our data sample 𝒮={xj,xj+,{ui,j}i=1N,{vi,j}i=1M}j=1T\mathcal{S}=\{x_{j},x_{j}^{+},\{u_{i,j}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{v_{i,j}\}_{i=1}^{M}\}_{j=1}^{T}. Let f|𝒮=(fk(xj),fk(xj+),{fk(ui,j)}i=1N,{fk(vi,j)}i=1M)j∈[T],k∈[d]∈ℝ(N+M+2)​d​Tf_{|\mathcal{S}}=(f_{k}(x_{j}),f_{k}(x_{j}^{+}),\{f_{k}(u_{i,j})\}_{i=1}^{N},\{f_{k}(v_{i,j})\}_{i=1}^{M})_{j\in[T],k\in[d]}\in\mathbb{R}^{(N+M+2)dT} be the restriction of ff onto 𝒮\mathcal{S}, using [T]={1,…,T}[T]=\{1,\ldots,T\}. Then ℛ𝒮​(ℱ)\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{F}) is defined as

ℛ𝒮(ℱ):=𝔼σsupf∈ℱ⟨σ,f|𝒮⟩\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{F})\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}=\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\langle\sigma,f_{|\mathcal{S}}\rangle (12)

where σ∼{±1}(N+M+1)​d​T\sigma\sim\{\pm 1\}^{(N+M+1)dT} are Rademacher random variables. Combining Theorem 3 and Lemma 4 with a concentration of measure argument yields the final generalization bound for debiased contrastive learning.

Theorem 5.

With probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, for all f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F} and N≥K−1N\geq K-1,

LSup​(f^)≤LDebiasedN,M​(f)+𝒪⁡(1τ−​1N+τ+τ−​1M+λ​ℛ𝒮​(ℱ)T+B​log⁡1δT)\displaystyle L_{\textnormal{Sup}}(\hat{f})\leq L_{\begin{subarray}{c}\textnormal{Debiased}\end{subarray}}^{N,M}(f)+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{\tau^{-}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}}+\frac{\tau^{+}}{\tau^{-}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{M}}+\frac{\lambda\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{F})}{T}+B\sqrt{\frac{\log{\frac{1}{\delta}}}{T}}\right) (13)

where λ=1(τ−)2​(MN+1)+(τ+)2​(NM+1)\lambda=\sqrt{\frac{1}{({\tau^{-}})^{2}}(\frac{M}{N}+1)+({\tau^{+}})^{2}(\frac{N}{M}+1)} and B=log⁡N⁡(1τ−+τ+)B=\log N\left(\frac{1}{\tau^{-}}+\tau^{+}\right).

The bound states that if the function class ℱ\mathcal{F} is sufficiently rich to contain some embedding for which LDebiasedN,ML_{\begin{subarray}{c}\textnormal{Debiased}\end{subarray}}^{N,M} is small, then the representation encoder f^\hat{f}, learned from a large enough dataset, will perform well on the downstream classification task. The bound also highlights the role of the positive and unlabeled sample sizes MM and NN in the objective function, in line with the observation that a larger number of negative/positive examples in the objective leads to better results [18, 2]. The last two terms in the bound grow slowly with NN, but the effect of this on the generalization error is small if the dataset size TT is much larger than NN and MM, as is commonly the case. The dependence on on NN and TT in Theorem 5 is roughly equivalent to the result in [1], but the two bounds are not directly comparable since the proof strategies differ.

7 Conclusion

In this work, we propose debiased contrastive learning, a new unsupervised contrastive representation learning framework that corrects for the bias introduced by the common practice of sampling negative (dissimilar) examples for a point from the overall data distribution. Our debiased objective consistently improves the state-of-the-art baselines in various benchmarks in vision, language and reinforcement learning. The proposed framework is accompanied by generalization guarantees for the downstream classification task. Interesting directions of future work include (1) trying the debiased objective in semi-supervised learning or few shot learning, and (2) studying the effect of how positive (similar) examples are drawn, e.g., analyzing different data augmentation techniques.

Broader Impact

Unsupervised representation learning can improve learning when only small amounts of labeled data are available. This is the case in many applications of societal interest, such as medical data analysis [5, 31], the sciences [22], or drug discovery and repurposing [38]. Improving representation learning, as we do here, can potentially benefit all these applications.

However, biases in the data can naturally lead to biases in the learned representation [29]. These biases can, for example, lead to worse performance for smaller classes or groups. For instance, the majority groups are sampled more frequently than the minority ones [16]. In this respect, our method may suffer from similar biases as standard contrastive learning, and it is an interesting avenue of future research to thoroughly test and evaluate this.

where a∧ba\wedge b denotes the minimum of two real numbers aa and bb.

−𝔼x∼px+∼px+{xi−}i=1N∼pN​[−log⁡h⁡(x,x+)h⁡(x,x+)+∑i=1Nh⁡(x,xi−)]≤e3/2​π2​N.\displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\quad-\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim p\\ x^{+}\sim p_{x}^{+}\\ \{x_{i}^{-}\}_{i=1}^{N}\sim p^{N}\end{subarray}}\bigg[-\log\frac{h(x,x^{+})}{h(x,x^{+})+\sum_{i=1}^{N}h(x,x_{i}^{-})}\bigg]\leq e^{3/2}\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2N}}.

limN→∞𝔼⁡[−log⁡ef​(x)T​f​(x+)ef​(x)T​f​(x+)+QN​∑i=1Nef​(x)T​f​(xi−)]\displaystyle\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[-\log\frac{e^{f(x)^{T}f(x^{+})}}{e^{f(x)^{T}f(x^{+})}+\frac{Q}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}e^{f(x)^{T}f(x_{i}^{-})}}\right]
=\displaystyle= 𝔼[limN→∞−logef​(x)T​f​(x+)ef​(x)T​f​(x+)+QN​∑i=1Nef​(x)T​f​(xi−)]\displaystyle\,\mathbb{E}\left[\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}-\log\frac{e^{f(x)^{T}f(x^{+})}}{e^{f(x)^{T}f(x^{+})}+\frac{Q}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}e^{f(x)^{T}f(x_{i}^{-})}}\right] (Dominated Convergence Theorem)
=\displaystyle= 𝔼⁡[−log⁡ef​(x)T​f​(x+)ef​(x)T​f​(x+)+Q​𝔼x−∼px−​ef​(x)T​f​(x−)].\displaystyle\,\mathbb{E}\left[-\log\frac{e^{f(x)^{T}f(x^{+})}}{e^{f(x)^{T}f(x^{+})}+Q\mathbb{E}_{x^{-}\sim p_{x}^{-}}e^{f(x)^{T}f(x^{-})}}\right].

𝔼x−∼px−​ef​(x)T​f​(x−)=τ−​(𝔼x−∼p​[ef​(x)T​f​(x−)]−τ+​𝔼x−∼px+​[ef​(x)T​f​(x−)]),\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x^{-}\sim p_{x}^{-}}e^{f(x)^{T}f(x^{-})}={\tau^{-}}(\mathbb{E}_{x^{-}\sim p}[e^{f(x)^{T}f(x^{-})}]-\tau^{+}\mathbb{E}_{x^{-}\sim p_{x}^{+}}[e^{f(x)^{T}f(x^{-})}]),

A.3 Proof of Theorem 3

In order to prove Theorem 3, which shows that the empirical estimate of the asymptotic debiased objective is a good estimate, we first seek a bound on the tail probability that the difference between the integrands of the asymptotic and non-asymptotic objective functions i slarge. That is, we wish to bound the probability that the following quantity is greater than ε\varepsilon:

Δ=|−log⁡h⁡(x,x+)h⁡(x,x+)+Q​g​(x,{ui}i=1N,{vi}i=1M)+log⁡h⁡(x,x+)h⁡(x,x+)+Q​𝔼x−∼px−​h​(x,x−)|,\displaystyle\Delta=\bigg|-\log\frac{h(x,x^{+})}{h(x,x^{+})+Qg(x,\{u_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M})}+\log\frac{h(x,x^{+})}{h(x,x^{+})+Q\mathbb{E}_{x^{-}\sim p_{x}^{-}}h(x,x^{-})}\bigg|,

where we again write h⁡(x,x¯)=expf​(x)⊤​f​(x¯)h(x,\bar{x})=\exp^{f(x)^{\top}f(\bar{x})}. Note that implicitly, Δ\Delta depends on x,x+x,x^{+} and the collections {ui}i=1N\{u_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} and {vi}i=1M\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M}. We achieve control over the tail via the following lemma.

Lemma A.2.

Let xx and x+x^{+} in 𝒳\cal X be fixed. Further, let {ui}i=1N\{u_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} and {vi}i=1M\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M} be collections of i.i.d. random variables sampled from pp and px+p_{x}^{+} respectively. Then for all ε>0\varepsilon>0,

ℙ⁡(Δ≥ε)≤2​exp⁡(−N​ε2​(τ−)22​e3)+2​exp⁡(−M​ε2​(τ−/τ+)22​e3).\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\Delta\geq\varepsilon)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{N\varepsilon^{2}(\tau^{-})^{2}}{2e^{3}}\right)+2\exp\left(-\frac{M\varepsilon^{2}(\tau^{-}/\tau^{+})^{2}}{2e^{3}}\right).

We delay the proof until after we prove Theorem 3, which we are ready to prove with this fact in hand.

Theorem 3.

For any embedding ff and finite NN and MM, we have

|L~DebiasedN​(f)−LDebiasedN,M​(f)|≤e3/2τ−​π2​N+e3/2​τ+τ−​π2​M.\displaystyle\left|\widetilde{L}_{\textnormal{Debiased}}^{N}(f)-L_{\begin{subarray}{c}\textnormal{Debiased}\end{subarray}}^{N,M}(f)\right|\leq\frac{e^{3/2}}{\tau^{-}}\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2N}}+\frac{e^{3/2}\tau^{+}}{\tau^{-}}\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2M}}.
Proof.

By Jensen’s inequality, we may push the absolute value inside the expectation to see that |L~UnbiasedN​(f)−LDebiasedN,M​(f)|≤𝔼​Δ|\widetilde{L}_{\textnormal{Unbiased}}^{N}(f)-L_{\begin{subarray}{c}\textnormal{Debiased}\end{subarray}}^{N,M}(f)|\leq\mathbb{E}\Delta. All that remains is to exploit the exponential tail bound of Lemma A​.2A.2.

To do this we write the expectation of Δ\Delta for fixed x,x+x,x^{+} as the integral of its tail probability,

𝔼​Δ=𝔼x,x+\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\ \Delta=\mathbb{E}_{x,x^{+}} [𝔼[Δ|x,x+]]=𝔼x,x+[∫0∞ℙ(Δ≥ε|x,x+)dε]\displaystyle\left[\mathbb{E}[\Delta|x,x^{+}]\right]=\mathbb{E}_{x,x^{+}}\left[\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathbb{P}(\Delta\geq\varepsilon|x,x^{+})\text{d}\varepsilon\right]
≤∫0∞2​exp⁡(−N​ε2​(τ−)22​e3)​d​ε+∫0∞2​exp⁡(−M​ε2​(τ−/τ+)22​e3)​d​ε.\displaystyle\leq\int_{0}^{\infty}2\exp\left(-\frac{N\varepsilon^{2}(\tau^{-})^{2}}{2e^{3}}\right)\text{d}\varepsilon+\int_{0}^{\infty}2\exp\left(-\frac{M\varepsilon^{2}(\tau^{-}/\tau^{+})^{2}}{2e^{3}}\right)\text{d}\varepsilon.

The outer expectation disappears since the tail probably bound of Theorem A.2 holds uniformly for all fixed x,x+x,x^{+}. Both integrals can be computed analytically using the classical identity

∫0∞e−c​z2​d​z=12​πc.\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-cz^{2}}\text{d}z=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{c}}.

Applying the identity to each integral we finally obtain the claimed bound,

2​e3​π(τ−)2​N+2​e3​π(τ−/τ+)2​M=e3/2τ−​2​πN+e3/2​τ+τ−​2​πM.\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{2e^{3}\pi}{(\tau^{-})^{2}N}}+\sqrt{\frac{2e^{3}\pi}{(\tau^{-}/\tau^{+})^{2}M}}=\frac{e^{3/2}}{\tau^{-}}\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{N}}+\frac{e^{3/2}\tau^{+}}{\tau^{-}}\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{M}}.

∎

We still owe the reader a proof of Lemma A.2, which we give now.

Proof of Lemma A.2.

We first decompose the probability as

ℙ⁡(|−log⁡h⁡(x,x+)h⁡(x,x+)+Q​g​(x,{ui}i=1N,{vi}i=1M)+log⁡h⁡(x,x+)h⁡(x,x+)+Q​𝔼x−∼px−​h​(x,x−)|≥ε)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\bigg(\bigg|-\log\frac{h(x,x^{+})}{h(x,x^{+})+Qg(x,\{u_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M})}+\log\frac{h(x,x^{+})}{h(x,x^{+})+Q\mathbb{E}_{x^{-}\sim p_{x}^{-}}h(x,x^{-})}\bigg|\geq\varepsilon\bigg)
=ℙ⁡(|log⁡{h⁡(x,x+)+Q​g​(x,{ui}i=1N,{vi}i=1M)}−log⁡{h⁡(x,x+)+Q​𝔼x−∼px−​h​(x,x−)}|≥ε)\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\bigg(\bigg|\log\big\{h(x,x^{+})+Qg(x,\{u_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M})\big\}-\log\big\{h(x,x^{+})+Q\mathbb{E}_{x^{-}\sim p_{x}^{-}}h(x,x^{-})\big\}\bigg|\geq\varepsilon\bigg)
=ℙ⁡(log⁡{h⁡(x,x+)+Q​g​(x,{ui}i=1N,{vi}i=1M)}−log⁡{h⁡(x,x+)+Q​𝔼x−∼px−​h​(x,x−)}≥ε)\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\bigg(\log\big\{h(x,x^{+})+Qg(x,\{u_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M})\big\}-\log\big\{h(x,x^{+})+Q\mathbb{E}_{x^{-}\sim p_{x}^{-}}h(x,x^{-})\big\}\geq\varepsilon\bigg)
+ℙ⁡(−log⁡{h⁡(x,x+)+Q​g​(x,{ui}i=1N,{vi}i=1M)}+log⁡{h⁡(x,x+)+Q​𝔼x−∼px−​h​(x,x−)}≥ε)\displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{P}\bigg(-\log\big\{h(x,x^{+})+Qg(x,\{u_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M})\big\}+\log\big\{h(x,x^{+})+Q\mathbb{E}_{x^{-}\sim p_{x}^{-}}h(x,x^{-})\big\}\geq\varepsilon\bigg)

where the final equality holds simply because |X|≥ε|X|\geq\varepsilon if and only if X≥εX\geq\varepsilon or −X≥ε-X\geq\varepsilon. The first term can be bounded as

ℙ⁡(log⁡{h⁡(x,x+)+Q​g​(x,{ui}i=1N,{vi}i=1M)}−log⁡{h⁡(x,x+)+Q​𝔼x−∼px−​h​(x,x−)}≥ε)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\bigg(\log\big\{h(x,x^{+})+Qg(x,\{u_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M})\big\}-\log\big\{h(x,x^{+})+Q\mathbb{E}_{x^{-}\sim p_{x}^{-}}h(x,x^{-})\big\}\geq\varepsilon\bigg)
=ℙ⁡(log⁡h⁡(x,x+)+Q​g​(x,{ui}i=1N,{vi}i=1M)h⁡(x,x+)+Q​𝔼x−∼px−​h​(x,x−)≥ε)\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\bigg(\log\frac{h(x,x^{+})+Qg(x,\{u_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M})}{h(x,x^{+})+Q\mathbb{E}_{x^{-}\sim p_{x}^{-}}h(x,x^{-})}\geq\varepsilon\bigg)
≤ℙ⁡(Q​g​(x,{ui}i=1N,{vi}i=1M)−Q​𝔼x−∼px−​h​(x,x−)h⁡(x,x+)+Q​𝔼x−∼px−​h​(x,x−)≥ε)\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}\bigg(\frac{Qg(x,\{u_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M})-Q\mathbb{E}_{x^{-}\sim p_{x}^{-}}h(x,x^{-})}{h(x,x^{+})+Q\mathbb{E}_{x^{-}\sim p_{x}^{-}}h(x,x^{-})}\geq\varepsilon\bigg)
=ℙ⁡(g⁡(x,{ui}i=1N,{vi}i=1M)−𝔼x−∼px−​h​(x,x−)≥ε⁡{1Q​h​(x,x+)+𝔼x−∼px−​h​(x,x−)})\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\bigg(g(x,\{u_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M})-\mathbb{E}_{x^{-}\sim p_{x}^{-}}h(x,x^{-})\geq\varepsilon\bigg\{\frac{1}{Q}h(x,x^{+})+\mathbb{E}_{x^{-}\sim p_{x}^{-}}h(x,x^{-})\bigg\}\bigg)
≤ℙ⁡(g⁡(x,{ui}i=1N,{vi}i=1M)−𝔼x−∼px−​h​(x,x−)≥ε​e−1).\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}\bigg(g(x,\{u_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M})-\mathbb{E}_{x^{-}\sim p_{x}^{-}}h(x,x^{-})\geq\varepsilon e^{-1}\bigg). (14)

The first inequality follows by applying the fact that log⁡x≤x−1\log x\leq x-1 for x>0x>0. The second inequality holds since 1Q​h​(x,x+)+𝔼x−∼px−​h​(x,x−)≥1/e\frac{1}{Q}h(x,x^{+})+\mathbb{E}_{x^{-}\sim p_{x}^{-}}h(x,x^{-})\geq 1/e. Next, we move on to bounding the second term, which proceeds similarly, using the same two bounds.

ℙ{−log(h(x,x+)+Qg(x,{ui}i=1N,{vi}i=1M)}+log{h(x,x+)+Q𝔼x−∼px−h(x,x−)}≥ε)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\bigg\{-\log\big(h(x,x^{+})+Qg(x,\{u_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M})\big\}+\log\big\{h(x,x^{+})+Q\mathbb{E}_{x^{-}\sim p_{x}^{-}}h(x,x^{-})\big\}\geq\varepsilon\bigg)
=ℙ⁡(log⁡h⁡(x,x+)+Q​𝔼x−∼px−​h​(x,x−)h⁡(x,x+)+Q​g​(x,{ui}i=1N,{vi}i=1M)≥ε)\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\bigg(\log\frac{h(x,x^{+})+Q\mathbb{E}_{x^{-}\sim p_{x}^{-}}h(x,x^{-})}{h(x,x^{+})+Qg(x,\{u_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M})}\geq\varepsilon\bigg)
≤ℙ⁡(Q​𝔼x−∼px−​h​(x,x−)−Q​g​(x,{ui}i=1N,{vi}i=1M)h⁡(x,x+)+Q​g​(x,{ui}i=1N,{vi}i=1M)≥ε)\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}\bigg(\frac{Q\mathbb{E}_{x^{-}\sim p_{x}^{-}}h(x,x^{-})-Qg(x,\{u_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M})}{h(x,x^{+})+Qg(x,\{u_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M})}\geq\varepsilon\bigg)
=ℙ⁡(𝔼x−∼px−​h​(x,x−)−g⁡(x,{ui}i=1N,{vi}i=1M)≥ε⁡{1Q​h​(x,x+)+g⁡(x,{ui}i=1N,{vi}i=1M)})\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\bigg(\mathbb{E}_{x^{-}\sim p_{x}^{-}}h(x,x^{-})-g(x,\{u_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M})\geq\varepsilon\bigg\{\frac{1}{Q}h(x,x^{+})+g(x,\{u_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M})\bigg\}\bigg)
≤ℙ⁡(𝔼x−∼px−​h​(x,x−)−g⁡(x,{ui}i=1N,{vi}i=1M)≥ε​e−1).\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}\bigg(\mathbb{E}_{x^{-}\sim p_{x}^{-}}h(x,x^{-})-g(x,\{u_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M})\geq\varepsilon e^{-1}\bigg). (15)

Combining equation (14) and equation (15), we have

ℙ⁡(Δ≥ε)≤ℙ⁡(|g⁡(x,{ui}i=1N,{vi}i=1M)−𝔼x−∼px−​h​(x,x−)|≥ε​e−1).\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\Delta\geq\varepsilon)\leq\mathbb{P}\bigg(\big|g(x,\{u_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M})-\mathbb{E}_{x^{-}\sim p_{x}^{-}}h(x,x^{-})\big|\geq\varepsilon e^{-1}\bigg).

We then proceed to bound the right hand tail probability. We are bounding the tail of a difference of the form |max⁡(a,b)−c||\max(a,b)-c| where c≥bc\geq b. Notice that |max⁡(a,b)−c|≤|a−c||\max(a,b)-c|\leq|a-c|. If a>ba>b then this relation is obvious, while if a≤ba\leq b we have |max⁡(a,b)−c|=|b−c|=c−b≤c−a≤|a−c||\max(a,b)-c|=|b-c|=c-b\leq c-a\leq|a-c|. Using this elementary observation, we can decompose the random variable whose tail we wish to control as follows:

|g⁡(x,{ui}i=1N,{vi}i=1M)−𝔼x−∼px−​h​(x,x−)|\displaystyle\big|g(x,\{u_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M})-\mathbb{E}_{x^{-}\sim p_{x}^{-}}h(x,x^{-})\big|
≤1τ−​|1N​∑i=1N𝔼x∼p​h​(x,ui)−𝔼x−∼px∼p​h​(x,x−)|+τ+τ−​|1M​∑i=1M𝔼x∼p​h​(x,vi)−𝔼x−∼px+x∼p​h​(x,x−)|\displaystyle\;\;\;\leq\frac{1}{\tau^{-}}\bigg|\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim p\end{subarray}}h(x,u_{i})-\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x^{-}\sim p\\ x\sim p\end{subarray}}h(x,x^{-})\bigg|+\frac{\tau^{+}}{\tau^{-}}\bigg|\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim p\end{subarray}}h(x,v_{i})-\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x^{-}\sim p_{x}^{+}\\ x\sim p\end{subarray}}h(x,x^{-})\bigg|

Using this observation, we find that

ℙ⁡(|g⁡(x,{ui}i=1N,{vi}i=1M)−𝔼x−∼px−​h​(x,x−)|≥ε​e−1)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\bigg(\big|g(x,\{u_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M})-\mathbb{E}_{x^{-}\sim p_{x}^{-}}h(x,x^{-})\big|\geq\varepsilon e^{-1}\bigg)
≤ℙ⁡(|1τ−​(1N​∑i=1Nef​(x)T​f​(ui)−τ+​1M​∑i=1Mef​(x)T​f​(vi))−𝔼x−∼px−​h​(x,x−)|≥ε​e−1)\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}\bigg(\big|\frac{1}{\tau^{-}}\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}e^{f(x)^{T}f(u_{i})}-\tau^{+}\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}e^{f(x)^{T}f(v_{i})}\right)-\mathbb{E}_{x^{-}\sim p_{x}^{-}}h(x,x^{-})\big|\geq\varepsilon e^{-1}\bigg)

where

I​(ε)=ℙ⁡(1τ−​|1N​∑i=1Nh⁡(x,ui)−𝔼x−∼p​h​(x,x−)|≥ε​e−12)\displaystyle\text{I}(\varepsilon)=\mathbb{P}\left(\frac{1}{\tau^{-}}\bigg|\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}h(x,u_{i})-\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x^{-}\sim p\end{subarray}}h(x,x^{-})\bigg|\geq\frac{\varepsilon e^{-1}}{2}\right)
II​(ε)=ℙ⁡(τ+τ−​|1M​∑i=1Mh⁡(x,vi)−𝔼x−∼px+​h​(x,x−)|≥ε​e−12).\displaystyle\text{II}(\varepsilon)=\mathbb{P}\left(\frac{\tau^{+}}{\tau^{-}}\bigg|\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}h(x,v_{i})-\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x^{-}\sim p_{x}^{+}\end{subarray}}h(x,x^{-})\bigg|\geq\frac{\varepsilon e^{-1}}{2}\right).

Hoeffding’s inequality states that if X,X1,…,XNX,X_{1},\ldots,X_{N} are i.i.d random variables bounded in the range [a,b][a,b], then

ℙ⁡(|1n​∑i=1NXi−𝔼​X|≥ε)≤2​exp⁡(−2​N​ε2b−a).\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\mathinner{\!\left\lvert\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_{i}-\mathbb{E}X\right\rvert}\geq\varepsilon\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{2N\varepsilon^{2}}{b-a}\right).

In our particular case, e−1≤h⁡(x,x¯)≤ee^{-1}\leq h(x,\bar{x})\leq e, yielding the following bound on the tails of both terms:

I​(ε)≤2​exp⁡(−N​ε2​(τ−)22​e3)andII​(ε)≤2​exp⁡(−M​ε2​(τ−/τ+)22​e3).\displaystyle\text{I}(\varepsilon)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{N\varepsilon^{2}(\tau^{-})^{2}}{2e^{3}}\right)\quad\text{and}\quad\text{II}(\varepsilon)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{M\varepsilon^{2}(\tau^{-}/\tau^{+})^{2}}{2e^{3}}\right).

∎

=𝔼𝒯∼𝒟​𝔼c∼ρ𝒯;x∼p(⋅|c)​[−log⁡ef(x)T𝔼x+∼p(⋅|c)f(x+)ef(x)T𝔼x+∼p(⋅|c)f(x+)+(K−1)𝔼ρ𝒯​(c−|c−≠h⁡(x))𝔼x−∼p(⋅|c−)ef​(x)T​f​(x−)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}\sim\mathcal{D}}\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}c\sim\rho_{\mathcal{T}};x\sim p(\cdot|c)\end{subarray}}\left[-\log\frac{e^{f(x)^{T}\mathbb{E}_{x^{+}\sim p(\cdot|c)}f(x^{+})}}{e^{f(x)^{T}\mathbb{E}_{x^{+}\sim p(\cdot|c)}f(x^{+})}+(K-1)\mathbb{E}_{\rho_{\mathcal{T}}(c^{-}|c^{-}\neq h(x))}\mathbb{E}_{x^{-}\sim p(\cdot|c^{-})}e^{f(x)^{T}f(x^{-})}}\right]

=𝔼𝒯∼𝒟​𝔼c∼ρ𝒯;x∼p(⋅|c)​[−log⁡exp⁡(f​(x)T​μc)exp⁡(f​(x)T​μc)+∑c−∈𝒯,c−≠cexp⁡(f​(x)T​μc−)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}\sim\mathcal{D}}\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}c\sim\rho_{\mathcal{T}};x\sim p(\cdot|c)\end{subarray}}\left[-\log\frac{\exp(f(x)^{T}\mu_{c})}{\exp(f(x)^{T}\mu_{c})+\sum_{c^{-}\in\mathcal{T},c^{-}\neq c}\exp(f(x)^{T}\mu_{c^{-}})}\right]

where the three inequalities follow from Jensen’s inequality. The first and third inequality shift the expectations 𝔼x+∼px,𝒯+\mathbb{E}_{x^{+}\sim p_{x,\mathcal{T}}^{+}} and 𝔼x−∼p(⋅|c−)\mathbb{E}_{x^{-}\sim p(\cdot|c^{-})}, respectively, via the convexity of the functions and the second moves the expectation 𝔼𝒯∼𝒟\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}\sim\mathcal{D}} out using concavity. Note that L¯Sup​(f)≤L¯Supμ​(f)\bar{L}_{\textnormal{Sup}}(f)\leq\bar{L}_{\textnormal{Sup}}^{\mu}(f) holds trivially. ∎

A.5 Proof of Theorem 5

We wish to derive a data dependent bound on the downstream supervised generalization error of the debiased contrastive objective. Recall that a sample (x,x+,{ui}i=1N,{vi}i=1M)(x,x^{+},\{u_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M}) yields loss

−log⁡{ef​(x)⊤​f​(x+)ef​(x)⊤​f​(x+)+N​g​(x,{ui}i=1N,{vi}i=1M)}\displaystyle-\log\left\{\frac{e^{f(x)^{\top}f(x^{+})}}{e^{f(x)^{\top}f(x^{+})}+Ng(x,\{u_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M})}\right\} =log⁡{1+N​g⁡(x,{ui}i=1N,{vi}i=1M)ef​(x)⊤​f​(x+)}\displaystyle=\log\left\{1+N\frac{g(x,\{u_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M})}{e^{f(x)^{\top}f(x^{+})}}\right\}

which is equal to ℓ⁡({f​(x)⊤​(f⁡(ui)−f⁡(x+))}i=1N,{f​(x)⊤​(f⁡(vi)−f⁡(x+))}i=1M)\ell\left(\left\{f(x)^{\top}\big(f(u_{i})-f(x^{+})\big)\right\}_{i=1}^{N},\left\{f(x)^{\top}\big(f(v_{i})-f(x^{+})\big)\right\}_{i=1}^{M}\right), where we define

ℓ⁡({ai}i=1N,{bi}i=1M)\displaystyle\ell(\{a_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{b_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M}) =log⁡{1+N​max⁡(1τ−​1N​∑i=1Nai−τ+​1M​∑i=1Mbi,e−1)}.\displaystyle=\log\left\{1+N\max\left(\frac{1}{\tau^{-}}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}a_{i}-\tau^{+}\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}b_{i},e^{-1}\right)\right\}.

To derive our bound, we will exploit a concentration of measure result due to [1]. They consider an objective of the form

Lu​n​(f)=𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡({f​(x)⊤​(f⁡(xi)−f⁡(x+))}i=1k)],L_{un}(f)=\mathbb{E}\left[\ell(\{f(x)^{\top}\big(f(x_{i})-f(x^{+})\big)\}_{i=1}^{k})\right],

where (x,x+,x1−,…,xk−)(x,x^{+},x^{-}_{1},\ldots,x^{-}_{k}) are sampled from any fixed distribution on 𝒳k+2\mathcal{X}^{k+2} (they were particularly focused on the case where xi−∼px^{-}_{i}\sim p, but the proof holds for arbitrary distributions). Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be a class of representation functions 𝒳→ℝd\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d} such that ‖f⁡(⋅)‖≤R\|f(\cdot)\|\leq R for R>0R>0. The corresponding empirical risk minimizer is

f^∈arg⁡minf∈ℱ​1T​∑j=1Tℓ⁡({f​(xj)⊤​(f⁡(xj​i)−f⁡(x+))}i=1k)\hat{f}\in\arg\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\,\frac{1}{T}\sum_{j=1}^{T}\ell\left(\{f(x_{j})^{\top}\big(f(x_{ji})-f(x^{+})\big)\}_{i=1}^{k}\right)

over a training set 𝒮={(xj,xj+,xj​1−,…,xj​k−)}j=1T\mathcal{S}=\{(x_{j},x_{j}^{+},x_{j1}^{-},\dots,x_{jk}^{-})\}_{j=1}^{T} of i.i.d. samples. Their result bounds the loss of the empirical risk minimizer as follows.

Lemma A.3.

[1] Let ℓ:ℝk→ℝ\ell\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\mathbb{R}^{k}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} be η\eta-Lipschitz and bounded by BB. Then with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta over the training set 𝒮={(xj,xj+,xj​1−,…,xj​k−)}j=1T\mathcal{S}=\{(x_{j},x_{j}^{+},x_{j1}^{-},\dots,x_{jk}^{-})\}_{j=1}^{T}, for all f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F}

Lu​n​(f^)≤Lu​n​(f)+𝒪⁡(η​R​k​ℛ𝒮​(ℱ)T+B​log⁡1δT)L_{un}(\hat{f})\leq L_{un}(f)+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{\eta R\sqrt{k}\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{F})}{T}+B\sqrt{\frac{\log{\frac{1}{\delta}}}{T}}\right)

where

ℛ𝒮(ℱ)=𝔼σ∼{±1}(k+2)​d​T[supf∈ℱ⟨σ,f|𝒮⟩],\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{F})=\mathbb{E}_{\sigma\sim\{\pm 1\}^{(k+2)dT}}\left[\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\langle\sigma,f_{|\mathcal{S}}\rangle\right],

and f|𝒮=(ft(xj),ft(xj+),ft(xj​1−),…,,ft(xj​k−))j∈[T]t∈[d]f_{|\mathcal{S}}=\left(f_{t}(x_{j}),f_{t}(x_{j}^{+}),f_{t}(x_{j1}^{-}),\dots,,f_{t}(x_{jk}^{-})\right)_{\begin{subarray}{c}j\in[T]\\ t\in[d]\end{subarray}}.

In our context, we have k=N+Mk=N+M and R=eR=e. So, it remains to obtain constants η\eta and BB such that ℓ⁡({ai}i=1N,{bi}i=1M)\ell(\{a_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{b_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M}) is η\eta-Lipschitz, and bounded by BB. Note that since we consider normalized embeddings ff, we have ‖f⁡(⋅)‖≤1\|f(\cdot)\|\leq 1 and therefore only need to consider the domain where e−1≤ai,bi≤ee^{-1}\leq a_{i},b_{i}\leq e.

Lemma A.4.

Suppose that e−1≤ai,bi≤ee^{-1}\leq a_{i},b_{i}\leq e. The function ℓ⁡({ai}i=1N,{bi}i=1M)\ell(\{a_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{b_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M}) is η\eta-Lipschitz, and bounded by BB for

η=e⋅1(τ−)2​N+(τ+)2M,B=𝒪⁡(log⁡N⁡(1τ−+τ+)).\eta=e\cdot\sqrt{\frac{1}{(\tau^{-})^{2}N}+\frac{(\tau^{+})^{2}}{M}},\quad\quad\quad B=\mathcal{O}\left(\log N\left(\frac{1}{\tau^{-}}+\tau^{+}\right)\right).

First, it is easily observed that ℓ\ell is upper bounded by plugging in ai=ea_{i}=e and bi=e−1b_{i}=e^{-1}, yielding a bound of

log⁡{1+N​max⁡(1τ−​e−τ+​e−1,e−1)}=𝒪⁡(log⁡N⁡(1τ−+τ+)).\displaystyle\log\left\{1+N\max\left(\frac{1}{\tau^{-}}e-\tau^{+}e^{-1},e^{-1}\right)\right\}=\mathcal{O}\left(\log N\left(\frac{1}{\tau^{-}}+\tau^{+}\right)\right).

To bound the Lipschitz constant we view ℓ\ell as a composition ℓ⁡({ai}i=1N,{bi}i=1M)=ϕ⁡(g⁡(ℓ⁡({ai}i=1N,{bi}i=1M))CLOSE\ell(\{a_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{b_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M})=\phi\left(g\left(\ell(\{a_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{b_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M}\right)\right) where11 1 Note the definition of gg is slightly modified in this context.,

ϕ⁡(z)=log⁡(1+N​max⁡(z,e−1)CLOSE\displaystyle\phi(z)=\log\left(1+N\max(z,e^{-1}\right)
g⁡({ai}i=1N,{bi}i=1M)=1τ−​1N​∑i=1Nai−τ+​1M​∑i=1Mbi.\displaystyle g(\{a_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{b_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M})=\frac{1}{\tau^{-}}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}a_{i}-\tau^{+}\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}b_{i}.

If z<e−1z<e^{-1} then ∂zϕ⁡(z)=0\partial_{z}\phi(z)=0, while if z≥e−1z\geq e^{-1} then ∂zϕ⁡(z)=N1+N​z≤N1+N​e−1≤e\partial_{z}\phi(z)=\frac{N}{1+Nz}\leq\frac{N}{1+Ne^{-1}}\leq e. We therefore conclude that ϕ\phi is ee-Lipschitz. Meanwhile, ∂aig=1τ−​N\partial_{a_{i}}g=\frac{1}{\tau^{-}N} and ∂big=τ+M\partial_{b_{i}}g=\frac{\tau^{+}}{M}. The Lipschitz constant of gg is bounded by the Forbenius norm of the Jacobian of gg, which equals

∑i=1N1(τ−​N)2+∑j=1M(τ+)2M2=1(τ−)2​N+(τ+)2M.\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{(\tau^{-}N)^{2}}+\sum_{j=1}^{M}\frac{(\tau^{+})^{2}}{M^{2}}}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{(\tau^{-})^{2}N}+\frac{(\tau^{+})^{2}}{M}}.

∎

Now we have control on the bound on ℓ\ell and its Lipschitz constant, we are ready to prove Theorem 5 by combining several of our previous results with Lemma A.3.

Theorem 5.

With probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, for all f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F} and N≥K−1N\geq K-1,

LSup​(f^)≤LSupμ​(f)≤LDebiasedN,M​(f)+𝒪⁡(1τ−​1N+τ+τ−​1M+λ​ℛ𝒮​(ℱ)T+B​log⁡1δT)\displaystyle L_{\textnormal{Sup}}(\hat{f})\leq L_{\textnormal{Sup}}^{\mu}(f)\leq L_{\begin{subarray}{c}\textnormal{Debiased}\end{subarray}}^{N,M}(f)+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{\tau^{-}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}}+\frac{\tau^{+}}{\tau^{-}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{M}}+\frac{\lambda\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{F})}{T}+B\sqrt{\frac{\log{\frac{1}{\delta}}}{T}}\right)

where λ=1τ−2​(MN+1)+τ+2​(NM+1)\lambda=\sqrt{\frac{1}{{\tau^{-}}^{2}}(\frac{M}{N}+1)+{\tau^{+}}^{2}(\frac{N}{M}+1)} and B=log⁡N⁡(1τ−+τ+)B=\log N\left(\frac{1}{\tau^{-}}+\tau^{+}\right).

Proof.

By Lemma 4 and Theorem 3 we have

Lsup​(f^)≤L~UnbiasedN​(f^)≤LDebiasedN,M​(f^)+e3/2τ−​π2​N+e3/2​τ+τ−​π2​M.\displaystyle L_{\textnormal{sup}}(\hat{f})\leq\widetilde{L}_{\textnormal{Unbiased}}^{N}(\hat{f})\leq L_{\begin{subarray}{c}\textnormal{Debiased}\end{subarray}}^{N,M}(\hat{f})+\frac{e^{3/2}}{\tau^{-}}\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2N}}+\frac{e^{3/2}\tau^{+}}{\tau^{-}}\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2M}}.

Combining Lemma A.3 and Lemma A.4, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, for all f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F}, we have

LDebiasedN,M​(f^)≤LDebiasedN,M​(f)+𝒪⁡(λ​ℛ𝒮​(ℱ)T+B​log⁡1δT),\displaystyle L_{\begin{subarray}{c}\textnormal{Debiased}\end{subarray}}^{N,M}(\hat{f})\leq L_{\begin{subarray}{c}\textnormal{Debiased}\end{subarray}}^{N,M}(f)+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{\lambda\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{F})}{T}+B\sqrt{\frac{\log{\frac{1}{\delta}}}{T}}\right),

where λ=η​k=1τ−2​(MN+1)+τ+2​(NM+1)\lambda=\eta\sqrt{k}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{{\tau^{-}}^{2}}(\frac{M}{N}+1)+{\tau^{+}}^{2}(\frac{N}{M}+1)} and B=log⁡N⁡(1τ−+τ+)B=\log N\left(\frac{1}{\tau^{-}}+\tau^{+}\right). ∎

A.6 Derivation of Equation (4)

In Section 4, we mentioned that the obvious way to approximate the unbiased objective is to replace px−p_{x}^{-} with px−​(x′)=(p⁡(x′)−τ+​px+​(x′))/τ−p_{x}^{-}(x^{\prime})=(p(x^{\prime})-\tau^{+}p_{x}^{+}(x^{\prime}))/\tau^{-} and then use the empirical counterparts for pp and px+p_{x}^{+}, and that this yields an objective that is a sum of N+1N+1 expectations. To give the derivation of this claim, let

ℓ⁡(x,x+,{xi−}i=1N,f)=−log⁡ef​(x)T​f​(x+)ef​(x)T​f​(x+)+∑i=1Nef​(x)T​f​(xi−).\displaystyle\ell(x,x^{+},\{x_{i}^{-}\}_{i=1}^{N},f)=-\log\frac{e^{f(x)^{T}f(x^{+})}}{e^{f(x)^{T}f(x^{+})}+\sum_{i=1}^{N}e^{f(x)^{T}f(x_{i}^{-})}}.

We plug in the decomposition as follows:

𝔼x∼p,x+∼px+{xi−}i=1N∼px−​[ℓ⁡(x,x+,{xi−}i=1N,f)]\displaystyle\quad\;\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim p,x^{+}\sim p_{x}^{+}\\ \{x_{i}^{-}\}_{i=1}^{N}\sim p_{x}^{-}\end{subarray}}[\ell(x,x^{+},\{x_{i}^{-}\}_{i=1}^{N},f)]
=∫p⁡(x)​px+​(x+)​∏i=1Npx−​(xi−)​ℓ​(x,x+,{xi−}i=1N,f)​d​x​d​x+​∏i=1Nd​xi−\displaystyle=\int p(x)p_{x}^{+}(x^{+})\prod_{i=1}^{N}p_{x}^{-}(x_{i}^{-})\ell(x,x^{+},\{x_{i}^{-}\}_{i=1}^{N},f)\text{d}x\text{d}x^{+}\prod_{i=1}^{N}\text{d}x_{i}^{-}
=∫p⁡(x)​px+​(x+)​∏i=1Np⁡(xi−)−τ+​px+​(xi−)τ−​ℓ​(x,x+,{xi−}i=1N,f)​d​x​d​x+​∏i=1Nd​xi−\displaystyle=\int p(x)p_{x}^{+}(x^{+})\prod_{i=1}^{N}\frac{p(x_{i}^{-})-\tau^{+}p_{x}^{+}(x_{i}^{-})}{\tau^{-}}\ell(x,x^{+},\{x_{i}^{-}\}_{i=1}^{N},f)\text{d}x\text{d}x^{+}\prod_{i=1}^{N}\text{d}x_{i}^{-}
=1(τ−)N​∫p⁡(x)​px+​(x+)​∏i=1N(p⁡(xi−)−τ+​px+​(xi−))​ℓ​(x,x+,{xi−}i=1N,f)​d​x​d​x+​∏i=1Nd​xi−.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(\tau^{-})^{N}}\int p(x)p_{x}^{+}(x^{+})\prod_{i=1}^{N}\left(p(x_{i}^{-})-\tau^{+}p_{x}^{+}(x_{i}^{-})\right)\ell(x,x^{+},\{x_{i}^{-}\}_{i=1}^{N},f)\text{d}x\text{d}x^{+}\prod_{i=1}^{N}\text{d}x_{i}^{-}.

By the Binomial Theorem, the product inside the integral can be separated into N+1N+1 groups corresponding to how many xi−x_{i}^{-} are sampled from pp.

(1)∏i=1Np⁡(xi−)\displaystyle\text{(1)}\quad\quad\prod_{i=1}^{N}p(x_{i}^{-})
(2)(N1)⁡(−τ+)​px+​(x1−)​∏i=2Np⁡(xi−)\displaystyle\text{(2)}\quad\quad\binom{N}{1}(-\tau^{+})p_{x}^{+}(x_{1}^{-})\prod_{i=2}^{N}p(x_{i}^{-})
(3)(N2)​∏j=12(−τ+)​px+​(xj−)​∏i=3Np⁡(xi−)\displaystyle\text{(3)}\quad\quad\binom{N}{2}\prod_{j=1}^{2}(-\tau^{+})p_{x}^{+}(x_{j}^{-})\prod_{i=3}^{N}p(x_{i}^{-})
⋯\displaystyle\cdots
(k+1)(Nk)​∏j=1k(−τ+)​px+​(xj−)​∏i=k+1Np⁡(xi−)\displaystyle\text{($k+1$)}\quad\quad\binom{N}{k}\prod_{j=1}^{k}(-\tau^{+})p_{x}^{+}(x_{j}^{-})\prod_{i=k+1}^{N}p(x_{i}^{-})
⋯\displaystyle\cdots
(N+1)∏i=1N(−τ+)​px+​(xi−)\displaystyle\text{($N+1$)}\quad\quad\prod_{i=1}^{N}(-\tau^{+})p_{x}^{+}(x_{i}^{-})

In particular, the objective becomes

1(τ−)N​∑k=0N(Nk)​(−τ+)k​𝔼x∼p,x+∼px+{xi−}i=1k∼px+{xi−}i=k+1N∼p​[−log⁡ef​(x)T​f​(x+)ef​(x)T​f​(x+)+∑i=1Nef​(x)T​f​(xi−)],\displaystyle\frac{1}{(\tau^{-})^{N}}\sum_{k=0}^{N}\binom{N}{k}(-\tau^{+})^{k}\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim p,x^{+}\sim p_{x}^{+}\\ \{x_{i}^{-}\}_{i=1}^{k}\sim p_{x}^{+}\\ \{x_{i}^{-}\}_{i=k+1}^{N}\sim p\end{subarray}}\left[-\log\frac{e^{f(x)^{T}f(x^{+})}}{e^{f(x)^{T}f(x^{+})}+\sum_{i=1}^{N}e^{f(x)^{T}f(x_{i}^{-})}}\right],

where {xi−}i=kj=∅\{x_{i}^{-}\}_{i=k}^{j}=\emptyset if k>jk>j. Note that this is exactly the Inclusion–exclusion principle. The numerical value of this objective is extremely small when NN is large. We tried various approaches to optimize this objective, but none of them worked.

Appendix B Experimental Details

CIFAR10 and STL10

We adopt PyTorch to implement SimCLR [2] with ResNet-50 [17] as the encoder architecture and use the Adam optimizer [23] with learning rate 0.0010.001 and weight decay 1​e−61e-6. We set the temperature tt to 0.50.5 and the dimension of the latent vector to 128128. All the models are trained for 400400 epochs. The data augmentation uses the following PyTorch code:

The models are evaluated by training a linear classifier with cross entropy loss after fixing the learned embedding. We again use the Adam optimizer with learning rate 0.0010.001 and weight decay 1​e−61e-6.

Imagenet-100

We adopt the official code22 2 https://github.com/HobbitLong/CMC/ for contrastive multiview coding (CMC) [40]. To implement the debiased objective, we only modify the “NCE/NCECriterion.py” file and adopt the rest of the code without change. The temperature of CMC is set to 0.070.07, which often makes the estimator 1τ−​(1N​∑i=1Nef​(x)T​f​(ui)−τ+​1M​∑i=1Mef​(x)T​f​(vi))\frac{1}{\tau^{-}}\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}e^{f(x)^{T}f(u_{i})}-\tau^{+}\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}e^{f(x)^{T}f(v_{i})}\right) less than e−1/te^{-1/t}. To retain the learning signal, whenever the estimator is less than e−1/te^{-1/t}, we optimize the biased loss instead. This improves the convergence and stability of our method.

Sentence Embedding

We adopt the official code33 3 https://github.com/lajanugen/S2V for quick-thought (QT) vectors [28]. To implement the debiased objective, we only modify the “src/s2v-model.py” file and adopt the rest of the code without changes. Since the official BookCorpus [25] dataset is missing, we use the inofficial version44 4 https://github.com/soskek/bookcorpus for the experiments. The feature vector of QT is not normalized, therefore, we simply constrain the estimator described in equation (7) to be greater than zero.

Reinforcement Learning

We adopt the official code55 5 https://github.com/MishaLaskin/curl of Contrastive unsupervised representations for reinforcement learning (CURL) [37]. To implement the debiased objective, we only modify the “curl-sac.py” file and adopt the rest of the code without changes. We again constrain the estimator described in equation (7) to be greater than zero since the feature vector of CURL is not normalized.
